_readme: Inputs for the Pests score (1.0-5.0, higher = less pest pressure). Rice: pressure is the brown planthopper (Nilaparvata lugens) temperature curve in `points` [temp_c, pressure 0-1], interpolated linearly: no development at 20 C or below, full pressure 25-30 C, none again at 35 C (Horgan et al. 2020, checked). Pressure is flat across the Mekong pins here (monthly means are 25.8-30.1 C in a typical year, April 0.98, and 26.3-31.6 C in an El Niño year, April 0.68 at Mỹ Xuyên and Ngã Năm), so rice does not separate sites; the score separates crops and months, and that is a decision, not an omission. Two constants have no numeric source and are team estimates (they cost one confidence level): shrimp `floor` (0.5, the lowest shrimp-phase pressure) and `break_weight` (0.5, the share of the rice pest cycle credited to a break crop). `hot_c` (35 C) is the existing heat rule, backed by the Kien Giang report; shrimp pressure = floor + (1 - floor) x min(hot days / days in the month, 1). There is no cold-snap rule: no source gives a drop or range that daily gridded data can count (research/cold-snap-shrimp.md). Upland pests are named per crop, with no numeric curve.

source.title: Horgan, Arida, Ardestani, Almazan (2020), PLoS ONE 15(6): e0235506, brown planthopper (Nilaparvata lugens) development and reproduction by temperature
source.note: Checked against the article text. Colony from Laguna, Philippines, reared at IRRI on IR22. Quotes: "did not develop to adults at 15 and 20°C"; "Nymphs failed to develop beyond the fourth instar at 35°C"; "egg-laying peaked at 30°C"; "the proportions of nymphs developing to adults before 15 days (0.87 ± 0.02)" (pooled 25 and 30°C). Philippine colony, not a Mekong one: applied here as the best published temperature curve.
